chapter_theme: The prologue praises the god who conquered the sum of his deeds and frees those who bow at his feet, announces the story of the red-eyed tall one who tore the lion, and asks the good to take the poet's lapses as the moon's spot is taken, naming his patron of the assembly and the old purana whose account he will follow.

cast.role: the Jain god the invocation praises as conqueror of the sum of deeds
the red-eyed tall one who tore the lion, hero of the story the poet begins

1.reading: The poet praises the one who conquered the whole sum of his deeds, whose knowledge spread wide, filled everything and lost nothing, and who now stands as a shining form in a ring of light; those who bowed at his feet were freed of their deeds and stand released.
1.nuance: The verse says that the devotees' deeds left them after they bowed (வினை நீங்கி நின்றார்) but does not say whether the bowing or the god's example does it; the god is praised for what he conquered, not for any giving. The verse does not name him; the Jain Arhat is read from வென்றான் வினையின் தொகை and from the next verse's link to the story's hero.

claims.claim: the god conquered the whole sum of karma by a knowledge that spread through all things
those who bow at his feet are freed of their karma

2.reading: The poet says the god stood as a light of the world above, having split fierce deeds, and that he begins the story of the red-eyed tall one, who in an earlier day went for refuge to him and who tore open the green-eyed lion with gaping mouth.
2.nuance: Line 1 அணிவான்சுடர் reads கணிவான்சுடர் in this text and may be a misprint. The grammar that joins the refuge (சரண் சென்ற மேனாள்) to the red-eyed tall one in line 4 is loose, so the hero's earlier refuge is the likely reading, not a fixed one. The hero is named only by epithet here; the Jain Vasudeva of the story is Tivittan.
2.event: Tivittan, the red-eyed tall one, tears open the lion (recalled as a feat of his past); the poet announces that he will tell his story.

claims.claim: the god split the fierce karma and stands as a light of the world above

3.reading: The poet says that, to tell the qualities of the tall one with the victorious discus, a desire has risen in him to spin a Tamil work here, and that if a flaw should come, great ones of knowledge are those who guard the lapses of people like himself.
3.nuance: நேமி நெடுமால் is the discus-bearing tall one, taken as the same hero as the செங்கண் நெடியான் of verses 2 and 5, and not as a god of worship; the Tamil does not say so here. அற்றங்கள் காப்பார் is guard the lapses, which is a different act from the Cintamani's washing of the flaw.

claims.claim: the wise guard the lapses of lesser people rather than exposing them

4.reading: The poet asks what fault there is in this speaking of excellence, since it was accepted by the discerning in the assembly of the king, Tirumal Nedunjendan, called lord of pure Tamil, with his victorious spear and cool garland.
4.nuance: Whether Tirumal Nedunjendan is the poet's patron, the king in whose assembly the work was first heard, or both is not fixed by the verse; கோமான் அவை may be his assembly or a king's assembly he belongs to. No claim rests on the identity.

5.reading: The poet says that even his fault, in the thought that told the story of the red-eyed tall one, is no fault before the good, as the moon's spot does not stop some from raising hands to it when it rises through the dark sky.
5.nuance: The moon's spot is used as an excuse in the same way in Neelakesi 6 and Civaka Cintamani 4; here it is the moon's rising before worshippers that matters, so the blemish is overlooked and not cleaned off.

claims.claim: the faults of a poet's work do not count before the good, as the moon's spot does not stop its worship

6.reading: The poet says that he will go by the account of the Purana of fair words, which came about because of the daughter of the Vidyadhara king, who is like a vanji creeper with anklets on her feet.
6.nuance: The verse gives the poem's source as an older purana and not as a tale of his own invention; the Vidyadhara king's daughter is the figure through whom that purana is said to have arisen, and is not an agent here. The verse names no purana.

links.note: Both open by praising the Jain god, but the Cintamani defines him by the bliss he reached by himself and his unceasing qualities, while the Soolamani defines him by the sum of deeds he conquered and by the freeing of those who bow.
links.teaches: One invocation names what the god is, the other what the god did to deeds, so the Jain epics share a god but each praises a different side of him.

links.note: Kural 10 has those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Soolamani 1 has those who bowed at the feet lose their deeds, after a god who conquered deeds himself.
links.teaches: The Kural says the feet carry one over births, and the Soolamani names a ground for it: a god who has himself overcome the deeds that bind.

gains.a: the departure of the devotees' deeds is set in the crossing-of-births frame that Tamil praise of the Lord's feet already uses, which the verse does not state
gains.b: the Lord's feet get a reason for their power, a victory over deeds, which the couplet leaves unsaid

links.note: Soolamani 1 praises a god who won the sum of deeds himself and lets those who bow be freed; Tirumanthiram 1649 says by Siva's grace deeds do not cling.
links.teaches: Release from deeds is credited to a conqueror's own victory in the Jain verse and to the giving of grace in the Saiva one, so the two differ over who removes the deeds.

gains.a: the god is seen as a conqueror who had deeds to overcome, not a giver, set against a Saiva grace that works without such a victory
gains.b: grace is seen against a god who earned the freedom by his own conquest, which makes the Saiva grace read as a gift and not a result

links.note: Both praise the Jain god as light: the Soolamani's light of the world above after splitting the deeds, the Cintamani's holy form that blazes brighter than flame.
links.teaches: The Soolamani's light is the result of cutting the deeds, while the Cintamani's is a body brighter than flame and marked with signs, so the same image names an act in one and a form in the other.

links.note: Both call the Jain god a lamp: the Soolamani's சுடர் that stands as the world's light after the deeds are split, the Neelakesi's ancient lamp of dharma who knows all things.
links.teaches: The lamp is the Soolamani's god in the world above, the Neelakesi's god as the source of dharma, so the image moves from where he stands to what he teaches.

links.note: Both poets ask the learned to deal with the flaws of the work, but the Cintamani asks that they wash the flaw out with their wit, while the Soolamani expects the wise to guard the lapses of people like himself.
links.teaches: One poet asks the reader to correct the flaw and the other to shield it, so the two Jain epics set different tasks for the learned in front of a faulty work.

links.note: Both place the work before an assembly of the discerning: the Soolamani says the discerning in the king's assembly accepted it, while the Cintamani says it was set out to be told to the assembly of the discerning.
links.teaches: The Soolamani states the assembly's acceptance as already given, where the Cintamani only offers the story for it, so one poet claims approval and the other asks for it.

links.note: Both poets answer the fear of fault with the moon's spot: the Neelakesi's poet says even the moon is not spotless and he will own a fault, the Soolamani's says the moon's spot does not stop some from worshipping it.
links.teaches: The Neelakesi's poet takes the blemish on himself, while the Soolamani's poet asks the good to look past it, so one image gives a confession in one work and a plea in the other.

links.note: Naladiyar 221 says the faults of those taken as good are kept within, as rice has its husk; Soolamani 5 asks that the poet's fault count for nothing before the good.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's rule keeping faults hidden between friends becomes a poet's plea that readers apply it to his own work, which turns a rule of friendship into a rule of reading.

gains.a: the plea to overlook a fault is given a rule behind it, a standing habit of the good to keep faults within
gains.b: the rule of keeping faults hidden is seen applied from a poet to his readers, outside the friendship it was written for

source_issues: Verse 2 line 1: the word கணிவான்சுடர் may be a misprint for அணிவான்சுடர்; the sense taken is a light of the world above.
Verse 4: whose assembly the king's assembly is (கோமான் அவை) is not settled by the text.
